analysis.one_liner: Bans political action committees from spending or raising money in federal elections.
analysis.headline: The bill had no cosponsors and died in the House Administration Committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite federal campaign law so that only candidates' own committees and political party committees could raise and spend money in federal elections. Every other organization that pools money to influence elections — political action committees, known as PACs — would be barred from contributing, soliciting, or spending to sway federal races. PACs today are how corporations, trade associations, labor unions, and ideological groups bundle large sums of money to lawmakers. The bill never went anywhere: it was referred to a House committee on the day it was introduced and never came back out.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters who believe legislative decisions are being shaped by organizations that bundle large campaign checks; candidates who rely on small individual donations rather than PAC money would compete on more equal terms. Members of Congress would lose a major, ready-made source of campaign funding, which would raise the cost of ignoring PAC money.

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds a new section to federal campaign law providing that no person other than an individual or a political committee may make, solicit, or receive contributions or make expenditures to influence a federal election [S3]. Because it also redefines 'political committee' to mean only candidates' principal campaign committees, party committees, and joint fundraising committees set up by candidates or parties, this excludes PACs from federal election activity entirely [S3].

By barring PACs, the bill would remove the main legal channel through which corporations, trade associations, labor unions, and other organized interests pool money to fund lawmakers' campaigns, reducing the influence of organized money over election outcomes [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: PACs themselves — corporate, trade association, union, and ideological PACs — would lose their ability to give to or spend in federal elections. Incumbent lawmakers who rely on PAC checks would have to raise money differently, and political fundraising consultants tied to the PAC system would lose business.

drawbacks.text: Critics of PAC bans argue that PACs are also how ordinary people pool small donations: union members, retirees, and members of ideological groups would lose a collective voice in elections, leaving only wealthy individuals and parties able to fund campaigns — an objection the bill's text does not answer [S3]. This is general knowledge about the policy mechanism, applied to the bill's structure [S3].

The bill contains no provision restricting money that moves outside the regulated channels, so large organized spending could shift to forms not covered by the definition — a common reason campaign-finance bans have historically proven easy to route around. The bill does briefly address a gap by treating committees controlled by candidates or officeholders as their authorized committees, closing one loophole in its own definitions [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The reform targets a real problem — organized money buying access and influence through PACs — but it is a blunt instrument. It would cut off the one channel ordinary people use collectively (union and ideological PACs funded by many small donors) while leaving individual wealth and unregulated spending channels intact. A better-designed version would address those routes as well. As written, the cost falls on all PACs equally, which serves concentrated interests but also takes away the pooled voice of union members and grassroots groups.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House committee that handles election law on the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Rob Portman introduced the bill on October 13, 1993 [S1] [S5].
That same day it was referred to the House Committee on House Administration, the committee with jurisdiction over federal election law [S5].
No further action was taken: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and the bill died when the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S5].
The bill attracted zero cosponsors over its life [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Organized interests that fund campaigns through PACs — corporations, trade associations, unions, and ideological groups — are better off, because the committee's inaction kept the PAC system untouched. Incumbent lawmakers who draw on PAC money also benefited from the bill never advancing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: PACs and the lawmakers they fund

for.name: Rep. Rob Portman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban PAC activity in federal elections.

against.name: House Committee on House Administration
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over federal election law
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and took no further action — no hearing or vote — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors, so no partisan split can be measured; the bill was introduced by a Republican and died in committee.

industries.note: These PACs pool corporate and industry money to fund the campaigns of federal lawmakers; a ban would end their federal election giving and the access it buys. The bill died, so their role in financing congressional campaigns was untouched.

Union PACs, funded by pooled member dues and small contributions, would also be barred from federal election activity. Unlike corporate PACs, they represent ordinary members pooling small sums, so the ban's cost to them is also a cost to organized working people.
An industry built around PAC formation, fundraising, and federal reporting would shrink if PACs were barred. Its loss would come from stricter rules rather than from harm to voters.
